# TO MR. MARCEL
## on his Book.
### QUATRAIN.

> Whoever reads the Author <note>Likely referring to Oswald Croll, whose work Marcel has translated or edited.</note> cannot understand him,
> Being in his secrets both mystical and obscure:

> He wished to make him easy to understand through his sound discourse.

->A. GAUDIN.<-

# TO MR. MARCEL
## on his Translation.

### S T A N Z A S.

*Crollius, through his learned book,* <note>Referring to Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609), a German physician and alchemist whose work was famously difficult to decipher.</note>
*Showed us his subtle spirit:*
*You, Marcel, by your clear writing,*
*Have sought to follow him above all others:*

*Why do I say follow? His figures* <note>original: "figures." In 17th-century alchemical texts, "figures" often referred to both numerical proportions and symbolic diagrams or emblems that were intentionally cryptic.</note>
*Were too obscure for everyone:*
*But you, to counter these blows,* <note>A metaphor for the frustration or intellectual "attacks" caused by a confusing text.</note>
*Have clarified his measures for us.* <term>mesures: the specific weights, proportions, and timing required for chemical "operations" or recipes.</term>

*Croll is the inventor, but the work*
*Covered in obscure enigmas,*
*Causes all authors to be despised,*
*Who do not clarify their language.*

*As for you, who are the interpreter*
*Of this treasure so precious,*
*May you gather the spoils of the Heavens:* <note>original: "butiner les Cieux." A poetic way of wishing Marcel either divine reward or the highest form of spiritual and intellectual success.</note>
*This is the happiness I wish for you.*

->I. BLANCHETESTE Surgeon.<-

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the commendatory poems written by Jean Marcel's friends to the formal legal document known as the "Privilege du Roy." This grant of copyright protection was essential for the publisher, Pierre Drobet, to secure his financial investment in this major translation of Oswald Croll’s alchemical work.</meta>

# Royal Privilege. <term>Privilege du Roy: A legal grant from the monarch providing a monopoly on the printing and sale of a specific book, serving as an early form of copyright protection.</term>

LOUIS, by the grace of God, King of France and of Navarre. To our beloved and faithful Councilors, the members of our Courts of Parliaments, Bailiffs, Seneschals, Provosts, their Lieutenants, and all our Justices and Officers to whom it shall concern, GREETINGS. Our well-beloved Pierre Drobet, Bookseller in our city of Lyon, has represented to us that he has recovered a book titled *Oswald Croll's Chemical Basilica* <note>original: "Osualdi Crolij Basilica Chymica." This was one of the most influential works of paracelsian medicine/alchemy of the era.</note>, which book he has had translated into French, titled *The Royal Chemistry of Crollius* <note>original: "La Royalle Chymie de Crollius"</note>, translated by Jean Marcel. The said petitioner would like to print this work for the utility and satisfaction of our subjects; but he fears that someone else might wish to print it or have it printed after he has incurred great expense for the said translation and printing, unless he possessed our letters of Privilege and Permission necessary for this. FOR THESE REASONS, we have permitted and do permit by these presents the said Drobet to print or have printed the said book, as many times and by such printer as he shall see fit, and to put and expose it for sale and distribute it, during the time and term of ten years. We forbid all printers, booksellers, book-vendors, and all our subjects of whatever quality and condition they may be, from printing or having printed the said book, both inside and outside the Kingdom, under the guise of any false mark, change of translation, or disguise whatsoever, without the consent and permission of the said Drobet or his representatives, under penalty of a fine of three hundred livres <note>The "livre" was the currency of France until 1795.</note>, half of which shall be paid to us and the other half to the said petitioner, along with the confiscation of all copies and all costs, damages, and interests owed to the said petitioner. This is granted on the condition of placing one copy in our public library in our city of Paris, according to our regulations. WE THEREFORE COMMAND YOU that you allow the said Drobet to enjoy the contents of these presents fully and peacefully, and to ensure that all others obey this decree. By placing these presents, or an extract thereof, at the beginning or end of the book, WE WILL that they be held as duly notified. And let full faith be given to copies signed by one of our beloved and faithful Councilors, Notaries, and Secretaries, as if it were the original. FOR SUCH is our pleasure. GIVEN at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, the seventeenth day of October, the year of Grace one thousand six hundred and twenty-three, and of our reign the fourteenth.

->By the King in his Council.<-

## RENOVARD.

->*And sealed with the great seal of yellow wax.*<-

<summary>A formal royal decree granted by King Louis XIII to the publisher Pierre Drobet, giving him exclusive rights to print and sell Jean Marcel’s French translation of Oswald Croll’s alchemical treatise for ten years.</summary>
<keywords>Louis XIII, royal privilege, copyright history, Pierre Drobet, Oswald Croll, alchemy, book trade, Lyon, 17th-century law</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of Oswald Croll’s work. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing how God (the "heavenly father") distributes light to all, justifying the author's decision to share his alchemical knowledge rather than keeping it secret.</meta>

<header>PREFACE</header>

...[those] among the others, to whom He has given the perfect knowledge of the truth amidst the greatest obscurity of darkness), I have wished to take the boldness not to bury in the dark caves of oblivion the talent that God has particularly wished to give me. This is because the doors of science always offer an opening to noble minds, whom the Muses themselves desire to serve willingly, in regard to their sincere curiosity. And in fact, it is an office of benign humanity to show the way to one who is wandering, and to keep in safety the one who has not yet gone astray. It is as such a person that I dare to qualify myself under divine favor, of which I am only a <term>secondary cause<note>In scholastic philosophy, God is the "First Cause" of all things, while humans act as "secondary causes" through whom God's will is enacted on Earth.</note></term> in this small publication. It is the

<margin>Some of these secrets which I had communicated to certain physicians were prepared for our Emperor Rudolf II <note>Rudolf II (1552–1612), Holy Roman Emperor, was a famous patron of the occult sciences, alchemy, and astronomy.</note>.</margin>

truth that I make a gift to you of these <term>spagyric<note>Spagyric (from Greek 'span' to draw out and 'ageirein' to gather) refers to alchemical medicine, specifically the process of separating and then recombining the essential elements of plants or minerals.</note></term> secrets drawn from the depths of my heart, so that you may use them for the benefit of your neighbor, and for the profit of the Spagyric school. Do not believe that these are frivolous inventions, as I assure you that I have had the curiosity to test them myself at my own expense; I give them to you, nonetheless, as new. I do not at all condemn those who say that contraries are healed by their contrary, provided that they do not look at the qualities <note>In traditional Galenic medicine, "qualities" referred to the four basic states: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, but only at the contrary virtues of nature, the goodness of which tends toward conservation, just as the malice of others occupies itself with the destruction of nature. Therefore, if the former seek to destroy, the latter are given for the relief of suffering nature; so that through their goodness, they may preserve the double goodness of nature, and chase away and expel the malice of the others. In this way, the contrary and adverse virtues of an evil nature are expelled and conquered by the goodness of the other nature.

But contrary qualities are not removed by other contrary qualities, seeing as they irritate one another and seem to stir themselves up for a combat, from which follows a greater infirmity rather than a strengthening of nature. This is because nature is not a quality, but rather a virtue <note>A "virtue" here refers to an innate power or spiritual essence, rather than just a physical temperature or state.</note>. Now, since it is a virtue, it does not demand aid and recourse from qualities to successfully fight its enemy. For it is not the physician who chases away the disease, but nature itself, which is the <term>mummy</term> <note>In the Paracelsian tradition, "mummy" refers to a vital, spiritual balm or life-force inherent in every living body that protects it from decay and disease.</note> or <term>internal balm</term>, which chases away the evil that is contrary to it—if (when its internal forces come to fail it) it receives (by means of the physician) external forces. And although the medicine may often be very good, it is better to commit the cure into the hands of nature without using any medicine at all.

PREFACE

### V.

### *The duty of the physician as a minister of nature.*

**J**Ust as the common definition of Philosophy does not depend solely on the judgment of Aristotle (as Pierre de la Ramée <note>Pierre de la Ramée (1515–1572), also known as Petrus Ramus, was a French humanist and logician who famously challenged the dominance of Aristotelian logic.</note> has very solidly shown), likewise (according to the testimony of Paracelsus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), known as Paracelsus, was a revolutionary Swiss physician who rejected traditional Galenic medicine in favor of chemical and mineral treatments.</note>) the light of nature has not been entirely exhausted by Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories on the four humors dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>: for we are no longer in the time of the Greeks, in which men drew natural light from one another, seeing as we have the power to discern and judge according to the scope of our own understanding; this is why he who desires to excel in the art of medicine must never stubbornly follow the opinion of a single sect (for in truth, no one can call themselves learned by following the opinion of only one master) but rather follow truth alone, having always before his eyes these verses by Horace <note>A French translation of a famous line from Horace’s *Epistles* (1.1.14): "Nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri."</note>,

> *Without fear, a courageous enemy of the North Wind <note>original: "Borée"; Boreas, the Greek god of the cold north wind.</note>*
> *I carry myself everywhere,*
> *And never under one master have I sworn my faith*
> *Who holds the upper hand.*

->AN EXHORTATION.<-

(in all branches of knowledge) in every family there is something remarkable which is not held in common with others. The same applies to books: for there is none so misguided that it does not contain something good within it, even if it is overlooked by the finest authors. Fabius <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–c. 100 AD), a Roman rhetorician whose works often touched on the education and development of the mind.</note> says that the previous age <margin>All secret things, by divine decree, must be revealed.</margin> studied the search for knowledge more than the one that followed; and while the sciences grow alongside our spirits, there are some who maliciously cast themselves into wretched errors, which are afterwards erased by the next generation. No, no, it is no longer the time for the treasures of wise nature to remain buried (the law being destined for all ages and nations until the completion of the age). The most speculative minds must employ all their efforts to master everything that presents itself to our senses. Nevertheless, it is very difficult—because of the brevity of human life—to be able to complete the circuit of nature and entirely comprehend all <margin>Daily experience, which has not yet reached its end, uncovers many of the errors of the ancients.</margin> her secrets. Now, the matter having been brought to this point, one must not totally reject the medicine of the ancients, nor that of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus.</note>. For if it must not be rejected, neither is there a need to embrace it totally, such that if someone has found something better, they should not be heard and followed: for each day teaches the next <note>original: "le iour enseigne le iour"; a French rendering of the Latin adage *dies docet diem*, suggesting that knowledge is cumulative and progressive.</note>, and the second is the master of the first. # A D M O N I T O R Y.

(as it is said) turned their backs on <term>methodical medicine</term> <note>The traditional medical system based on the teachings of Galen and Avicenna, which relied on balancing "humors" through theoretical logic.</note>, should never be placed in parallel with Paracelsus, who follows nothing that is not in accordance with reason and experience; as is well-demonstrated by those who are enlightened by intellectual light. In fact, we should never be so stubborn regarding the authority of a single individual that we place truth after him, without which all authorities are harmful and of no value, according to the judgment of the wise. They assure us that one must not look so much at the authority of those speaking, but rather if what they say conforms to truth; furthermore, when reporting the opinions of others, one must take care not to add anything of one's own invention.

The true method consists in the knowledge and cure of the disease: knowing what regimen of life and what medication are proper for driving out the disease and restoring health. This is why <term>Wimpinaeus</term> <note>Johann Albrecht Wimpinaeus (16th century), a physician who wrote in defense of Paracelsian chemical medicine.</note> demonstrates most learnedly how the <term>Paracelsians</term> <note>Physicians who followed the "Spagyric" or chemical path of Paracelsus, focusing on minerals and metals rather than just herbs.</note> cure great illnesses in three ways.

The first is that diseases are now better understood; for in ancient times, they were all attributed to the <term>four humors</term> <note>The traditional theory that health was determined by the balance of four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>. This is why they could not be cured; the reason being the <term>tartar</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "tartar" refers to stony or crystalline deposits in the body—such as kidney stones or gout—which Paracelsus believed were caused by impurities in food and drink "precipitating" inside the organs.</note> adhering to one of the limbs, which cannot be referred to any of the four humors. But since we are now discussing tartar, it seems right to me to discuss it at length.

In truth, I cannot marvel enough that many great men of our century consume their time and money on the promises of certain wicked imposters, who ordinarily roam the countryside to ensnare the simple credulity of people of good faith. Why should one not think that it is impossible to acquire any perfection of these mysteries without the **liberal arts**? <note>The "liberal arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy) were considered the essential foundation for any advanced study, including alchemy.</note> And often such charlatans and **Philosophisters** <term>Philosophisters</term> <note>original: "Philosophistes"; a derogatory term for those who pretend to be philosophers but are actually frauds or "puffers" who only follow recipes without understanding principles.</note> have not tasted even the smallest drop from the fountains of nature, contenting themselves with their fantastical and frantic inventions, accompanied by a sea of words with which they enrich the ears of those too credulous of their discourse. And so that those who have little money might place their small pouch in their hands, they promise them mountains and wonders, and do nothing but lie, keeping no other promise to these poor credulous souls than new and more subtle inventions after having deceived them three or four times. If I were believed, one would love the company of such people as much as the pains of hell.

<margin>These sophistries aim at no other end than profit; likewise, the end for such "sellers of smoke" <note>A classical idiom for people who sell false promises or non-existent influence.</note> is nothing but fire or ashes.</margin>

And thus playing out the fable of **Pandora**, <note>In Greek mythology, Pandora's box released all the evils into the world; here it signifies that these frauds bring only trouble and ruin.</note> nothing else has happened to them but what **Alphidius** <note>An author often cited in alchemical literature, usually identified as an Arab philosopher.</note> had predicted: for having consumed their brains by means of **circulation**, <term>circulation</term> <note>A process where a liquid is heated so that it rises as vapor and falls back as liquid repeatedly in a closed vessel.</note> they have found only color for a tincture, and for the Hermetic stone, nothing but pebbles.

### *Observations.*

<margin>
I.
If one pours and adds too small a quantity of oil of vitriol, at the very least it causes and brings about vomiting.
</margin>
In pouring the oil of vitriol, you must observe a certain method, for fear that the flavor of the salt becomes too sour through too strong a reaction <note>original: *repercussion*; referring to the chemical feedback or intensity of the neutralization.</note>, and that it provokes vomiting; for if you put too much oil of vitriol in, it will not purge; but it will act through the four emunctories <term>emunctories</term> <note>The body's natural waste-disposal organs or channels, such as the kidneys, skin, and bowels.</note>, mixed with the purgative; namely, through vomiting, stools, urine, and sweat.

<margin>II.</margin>
If the pouring can be done through a funnel that has a very narrow opening—so that by some artifice the drops of the oil of vitriol distill gently into the oil of tartar—it will be the most certain way. For in this fashion, the most subtle spirits that rise through the mutual boiling <note>The effervescence or bubbling produced by the chemical reaction between the acid and the base.</note> which occurs during the violent mixture are retained.

<margin>III.</margin>
Note that the glass heats up greatly by the conjunction of these two fires in this mutual boiling. Here one can make a remark regarding epilepsy; for when the spirit of life is agitated in the body by heterogeneous or dissimilar parts, it boils in this same fashion. <note>Crollius uses the chemical reaction in the glass as a metaphor for a seizure, where the "vital spirits" react violently to "foreign" matter in the body.</note>

The digestive <note>A preparation intended to aid digestion or "ripen" humors in the body to prepare them for evacuation.</note> of this tartar of vitriol, which must necessarily be added to purgative medicines beforehand, can be made in this way:

### *Emetic.* <note>A substance used to induce vomiting, a common practice in early modern medicine to rid the body of "corrupt humors."</note>

The properties of antimony, vitriol, and hellebore hold the first rank for the provocation of vomiting; for they leave nothing bad within the ventricle <note>The stomach.</note>, but rather completely overturn all the impurities found therein.

The hellebore emetic can be found in the works of Conradinus, a most expert physician, in the book he wrote on the *Hungarian Fever* <note>original: "Febri Vngarica"; a severe fever often associated with typhus that affected soldiers in 16th-century Hungary.</note>. # THE ROYAL CHEMISTRY

### *The method for properly precipitating Mercury.*

Take half a pound of well-purified Mercury, to which you will add one pound of **oil of sulfur** <note>In the 17th century, "oil of sulfur" referred to sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur under a glass bell.</note>, made and rectified by the bell method. This oil is used because it precipitates the Mercury with more certainty than **oil of vitriol** <note>Another form of sulfuric acid, typically derived from iron or copper sulfates.</note> or any other corrosive oil whatsoever; furthermore, it **coagulates** <note>In alchemy, to "coagulate" is to turn a liquid or vaporous substance into a solid form.</note> it in such a way that it can endure a greater heat. You will therefore put these two things together (namely the Mercury and the oil of sulfur) in **digestion** <note>The process of steeping a substance in a liquid at a gentle, steady heat.</note> for the space of two full days in a **sand-bath** <note>A container of sand heated by a fire, used to provide even, indirect heat to a glass vessel.</note>. After that, you will distill them in a well-**luted** <term>retort</term> <note>A "retort" is a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation. "Luting" refers to sealing the joints with a clay-like paste to prevent vapors from escaping.</note>, provided that your distillation is slow, **rectifying** <note>Purifying a liquid by repeated distillation.</note> the extract until the fourth time, and no more, because at the fourth time it is necessary to add more oil of sulfur. Then, strengthen the fire until the retort becomes entirely red-hot; by this means, you will have your precipitated Mercury in a white mass at the bottom of the retort, which you will break to draw it out. It must then be ground upon the marble with hot and distilled rainwater, which removes the salt from the precipitate, making it tasteless. Afterward, place your Mercury in a glass vessel that is very wide at the neck and fill it with the said water, washing and stirring it for the space of four hours, or until the water comes out fresh. I do not say that one must always use the first water poured: for having washed it for a little time with the

### *Observations on the signs of true precipitated Mercury.*

<margin>I.</margin> The authenticity of precipitated Mercury is recognized if it is ground with **gold**, and the gold does not whiten at all, but remains in its first and natural color. <note>Mercury typically forms a white amalgam when it touches gold; if it has been properly converted into an oxide (precipitated), it loses this ability.</note>

<margin>II.</margin> It is not necessary for the true precipitate to be totally **fixed** <note>In alchemy, "fixed" means a substance that can withstand fire without evaporating. Here, Crollius argues some volatility is needed for it to work as medicine.</note>, for if that were so, it would have no power or **purgative faculty**.

<margin>III.</margin> There is no fixed precipitate which cannot be **reduced** <note>Turned back into liquid, metallic mercury.</note>, for (as I have said above) if it were otherwise, it could not operate on the human body, insofar as its operations depend on its **rawness** <note>original: "crudité." In this context, it refers to the chemical activity or potency of the substance that has not been completely neutralized by "fixation."</note>.

### *The powers of precipitated Mercury.*

This Mercury is the true natural balm, which possesses the **incarnative** <note>A medical term referring to the power to heal wounds and promote the growth of new flesh.</note> virtue, which renews and purifies the human body of all impurities and **venereal infections**: for when the entire mass of the blood is corrupted and filled with various seeds of disease, it cannot change its condition for the better except by means of **softened Mercury** <note>Mercury that has been processed (often with acids and heat) to be less corrosive and more "sweet" or safe for internal use.</note>, which alone has the strength to act in such a case.

<margin>I.</margin> It is a most excellent remedy against all sorts of diseases caused by the **putrefaction of the humors** <note>Pre-modern medicine held that health was a balance of four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile); disease was caused when these fluids "rotted" or became imbalanced.</note>, and one can hardly find a...

# OF CROLLIUS

<margin>XI</margin> [it is] a swifter remedy for diseases already deemed hopeless.

<margin>II.</margin> It draws out all the bad humors of the body and the discharges <note>original: "defluxions." In humoral medicine, these were considered excess fluids flowing from the brain to other parts of the body, causing illness.</note> of the brain.

### *The use of precipitated Mercury.*

<margin>I.</margin> For **gout**, it is given with **pills of Rufus** <note>A famous historical compound, also known as "pillulae communes," usually made of aloes, myrrh, and saffron.</note> and oil of honey.

<margin>II.</margin> It is wonderful against **pleurisy** <note>Inflammation of the lining of the lungs.</note> when given with a specific vehicle <note>In pharmacy, a "vehicle" is an inactive substance used to carry or deliver the active medicine.</note>.

<margin>III.</margin> It is effective against poisons and **scabies** <note>original: "la rogne," a contagious skin disease.</note>.

<margin>IV.</margin> It is admired for treating continuous and intermittent fevers, by adding four or five drops of **oil of vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid.</note> along with the pills of Rufus.

<margin>V.</margin> It is a true **catholicon** <note>A "universal remedy" or a "cure-all."</note> for the cure of **syphilis** <note>original: "la verolle," also known as the Great Pox.</note>, and for this disease alone it deserves to be called a **root-cutter** <note>original Greek: ῥιζοτόμον (rhizotomon). While this term originally referred to herb-gatherers or "root-cutters," Crollius uses it metaphorically for a medicine that "uproots" a disease.</note>, since it uproots all venomous and venereal ulcers, or similar discharges, when the dose is repeated.

<margin>VI.</margin> It is impossible to find any remedy more excellent for **jaundice** <note>original: "iauniſſe ou icterie."</note>.

<margin>VII.</margin> Its use is also required in times of **plague**, together with the pestilential pills of Rufus.

<margin>VIII.</margin> It is greatly purgative, which is why it is used for the cleansing of foul-smelling ulcers.

<margin>IX.</margin>
Whenever **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> wished to cure the **pox** <note>original: "la verolle," referring to syphilis.</note>, he used it with an **electuary** <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powder with honey or syrup.</note> of rose juice. **Phoedrus** <note>likely Georgius Phaedro, a 16th-century Paracelsian physician.</note> did not do this, for he mixed it with **spirit of tartar** <note>A solution of potassium carbonate or a related derivative of wine-barrel deposits, used in alchemy.</note>; and indeed, he asserts that with this single remedy he chased away and expelled every kind of venereal pustule.

### *The dose of precipitated Mercury.*

<margin>V.</margin>
One must first have regard for the constitution of the body; for to the strongest and most robust, one may give up to six grains; to the smallest, three; and thus the average person will have a moderate amount, according to the judgment of the wise Physician.

<margin>IV.</margin>
It can be administered with appropriate pills: for headaches, with **pills of Cochiis** <note>A traditional purgative pill containing aloes, colocynth, and scammony.</note>; for pains in the arms, with **hermodactyl pills** <note>original: "pillules hermodatt," made from a plant used historically to treat gout and joint pain.</note>, or mixed with purgative extracts.

<margin>III.</margin>
It works much better with liquorice juice than with **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient "universal" medicine containing dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</note>; it is also administered—

<margin>II.</margin>
—with conserve of roses, or with rose sugar, or else wrapped in **singing bread** <note>original: "pain à chanter," thin wafers identical to communion hosts, used by apothecaries to wrap bitter medicines for swallowing.</note>—

<margin>I.</margin>
—in a silver spoon half full of wine, the better to make it go down.

## *The Coralline Secret of Paracelsus, or Non-Corrosive Red Sublimated Mercury.*

Take one pound of Mercury which has been well purged with a lye of quicklime, or potash <note>original: "cendres clavellées," literally "gravelled ashes," a high-quality potassium carbonate used in early chemistry.</note> at least six or seven times; then wash it afterwards with common salt and vinegar until it turns a celestial [sky-blue] color, for then it will be ready for sublimation.

Take one pound of this Mercury; of saltpeter purged as you will see below; and of vitriol <note>A term for various metal sulfates; here likely referring to iron or copper sulfate.</note> calcined until it is red, <term>equal parts of each</term> <note>original Latin: "ana," a standard pharmaceutical abbreviation meaning an equal weight of each ingredient mentioned.</note> two pounds. Let the whole be pulverized and well mixed together; afterward, you must sprinkle your mixture with distilled vinegar—choosing the strongest that can be found—and then incorporate it all together with a wooden pestle. You must continue the action until the Mercury is well mortified <note>In alchemy, to "mortify" mercury means to grind it with other substances until its metallic luster disappears and it is "killed" into a dull powder.</note>. Once this is done, you must immediately make a mass of the whole and place it in a medium-sized retort <note>original: "cornue," a glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling liquids or gases.</note> that is well-luted <note>Sealed with "lute," a protective paste of clay and binders used to make joints airtight and protect the glass from direct flame.</note>, having taken care that it is very clean; I mean that there should be no grit in the glass, for that would cause it to break. 

These things being well observed, you shall perform your distillation in a sand bath for the space of an entire night, so that the phlegm <note>The watery, inactive portion of the distilled liquid.</note> of the vinegar may come out. Once the phlegm has come out, the fire must be increased by degrees for twenty-four hours, for the Mercury will then rise to the highest part of the retort, turning a blackish color; as for the yellow powder, it will remain in the middle of the retort, and slightly lower, above the dregs <note>original: "feces," the solid waste or residue remaining at the bottom of the vessel after distillation.</note>.

### *Note on the purification of saltpeter.*

To know if the saltpeter <note>original: "sel petre." Potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in alchemical preparations and gunpowder.</note> of which we spoke above is well purified, one must proceed in this manner: namely, take some of the said saltpeter and place it on an iron plate, then set fire to it. If the salt flies away <note>The substance should "flash" or deflagrate without leaving solid residue if pure.</note> without leaving any dirty trace, it is a sign that it is well purified; if, on the contrary, it leaves the plate or sheet dirty and blackish, it is not, and in this case, it must be purified further.

### *Butyrous Flowers of Antimony.*

### *The method for removing the corrosion.*

We have already said that this liquor is greatly corrosive; however, it can be softened and corrected in this way: namely, by washing it several times with hot water, which dissolves the spirits of salt <note>original: "esprits du sel." This refers to the acidic residues—hydrochloric acid—produced during the chemical reaction.</note> from which the corrosion proceeds. This powder must be preserved for use on those with strong constitutions <note>original: "fortes complexions." In early medicine, a person's "complexion" or "constitution" determined how they reacted to powerful drugs.</note>; and in fact, it is better than the flowers of Antimony <note>A "flower" in alchemy refers to a fine powder produced by sublimation (heating a solid until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again) or precipitation.</note> prepared by sublimation.

It is permitted for anyone who wishes to rectify <note>To purify a liquid by repeated distillation.</note> this Antimonial butter, or Mercury of Life <note>original: "Mercure de vie." A name given to this preparation by the famous physician Paracelsus; it is chemically antimony oxychloride.</note>, before pouring the hot water onto it, as by this means he will obtain whiter flowers; those who know how to rectify this oil with fermented and rarefied gold can give assurance as to whether it is useful for chemical medicine.

### *The use and powers of the buttery flowers of Antimony.*

<margin>I.</margin> It is very good against the plague.
Against headaches, in whatever manner they arise.
Against fevers (if by chance they provoke vomiting), there is no need to fear that it will cause any harm.
For the pox <note>original: "verolle." Historically, this usually refers to the "Great Pox," or syphilis.</note>.
For leprosy.
For dropsy <note>original: "hydropifie." A condition characterized by an accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities, now known as edema.</note>, it most often performs its operations through the lower parts <note>i.e., it acts as a laxative rather than an emetic.</note>, and not by vomiting.
For malignant and long-standing ulcers.

### Restorative

This restorative is internally and naturally <term>corroborative</term> <note>From the Latin *corroborare*, meaning to strengthen or invigorate.</note>; besides which, it is a balm that <term>mondifies</term> <note>Cleanses or purifies.</note> and clarifies the spirits and elements of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>A term for the human body, which alchemists believed mirrored the "Macrocosm" or the entire universe.</note>. ## *Salt of Coral.*

The salt of coral must be purified in the same way as that of the shells that bear pearls, or as <term>crayfish eyes</term> <note>original: *yeux d'escrivisse*. These are gastroliths—small, stony concretions of calcium carbonate found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine as an antacid.</note> and other crusty and scaly stones. All these salts dissolve in the months of June, July, and August in cool cellars, upon porphyry or marble slabs, or indeed glass tables, for then they are cooler because of the <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>An ancient philosophical and physical concept where the qualities of a substance are intensified by the presence of their opposite. Here, the internal cold of the cellar is supposedly increased by the external heat of summer.</note> of the cellar; and I do not think one can succeed at any other time than those I have stated.

No one has yet been able to see the true and essential <term>tincture</term> <note>An extract of a substance, usually dissolved in alcohol, intended to capture its essential medicinal properties.</note> of coral; for that which many believe to be the best and true one, which is made with an infusion of <term>honey water</term> <note>A solvent made from the distillation of honey, prized for its supposed ability to extract "souls" from minerals.</note>, is instead the tincture of the honey rather than of the coral. There are many solvents which (if they remain for some time in <term>digestion</term> <note>A process of keeping a substance in a state of gentle, constant heat to encourage chemical breakdown or extraction.</note>) turn red of their own accord, as is apparent from frequently rectified spirit of turpentine; and by this means, those who sell it deceive those who are not well-advised; inasmuch as they believe they have the tincture of the dissolved thing, yet they have nothing but the solvent. Even <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>Distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note> poured over salt of coral, although it turns red during digestion, does not nonetheless acquire the true redness.

It stops putrefaction, strengthens the heart and the <term>vital spirits</term> <note>In early modern medicine, these were thought to be refined substances that traveled through the body to sustain life and movement.</note>, and defends them against venom.

...stones, Crystal & pebbles, are prepared in this fashion.

To obtain this liquor, one must first burn three or four times the said stones, having been turned to powder; the burning is performed thus: take **native sulfur** <note>original: "soulphre vif"; naturally occurring sulfur, also known as brimstone.</note>, put it into a **crucible** with the aforementioned powder; and cover your crucible immediately. This **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical constitution.</note> is performed by the **wheel fire** <note>original: "feu de la rouë"; a circular fire built around a crucible to provide even, intense heat.</note>; towards the end, cover your crucible with coals, so that the fire is on all sides, for by this means the sulfur is cleansed and purified; the **dregs** <note>original: "feces"; in alchemy, this refers to the solid sediment or waste left after a process.</note> which are at the bottom must be crushed and mixed with an equal amount of purified **saltpeter** <note>original: "sel nitre"; potassium nitrate, used as a powerful oxidizing agent.</note>; this being done, one must calcine the said dregs in a covered pot by the wheel fire, so that they become liquid; the salt from the said dregs must be washed with hot water because of the corrosion, and then immediately **dulcified** <note>original: "adoucy/dulcification"; the process of washing away salts or acids to make a substance "sweet" or non-corrosive.</note>; which being done, you shall have in hand the **menstruum of Turpentine** <note>original: "menstruë Terebenthine"; in alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent used to dissolve solids.</note> which you shall pour into your matter, stirring it diligently, lest it harden and turn back into stone; and by this means your work shall be dissolved to your satisfaction. As for the menstruum, it must afterwards be drawn off by the **alembic** <note>A classic distillation apparatus consisting of two retorts connected by a tube.</note>, so as to have no difficulty in the dulcification of the salt which remains at the bottom, which is done with distilled water, which must afterwards be removed by evaporation, or by the **filter**; repeating this two or three times, you shall have your salt, which will resolve into liquor when placed in a damp cellar, upon a marble slab, during the aforementioned months. ### THE COMPOSITION

Take, for example, two or three pounds of turpentine, & pour them into two pounds of **distilled vinegar**; these things, thus mixed, shall be distilled according to the art, in a **sand bath** <note>original: "au sable"; heating a vessel by placing it in a container of sand to ensure even temperature.</note>, observing the degrees of the fire, until the vinegar has come forth with the **spirit of turpentine**; when you see that very little spirit is coming out, it is a sign that you must increase the fire, so that the oil comes out, which you shall recognize by its yellow color. As for the water that comes out with the oil, it is red & very sour; continue your distillation until the oil begins to come out red, and then you shall stop. The separations shall be made in a glass funnel; remember also to separate the vinegar because it must be **rectified** <note>Purified or concentrated by repeated distillation.</note> with ginger.

One must have a quantity of distilled vinegar, for at the same time one can dissolve all the stones that **Paracelsus** <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals in medicine.</note> attributes to the cure of **the stone** <note>original: "calcul"; refers to kidney or bladder stones.</note>, which produce great effects therein, as we shall say hereafter.

### Oil of cinnamon.

**Oil of cinnamon**, prepared as it should be, deserves to be placed among the most admirable **spagyric** <note>The alchemical practice of separating, purifying, and recombining the "essences" of plants or minerals to create potent medicine.</note> **restoratives** <note>original: "confortatifs"; medicines intended to strengthen the organs or vital spirits.</note>.

And although every **chemist** <note>original: "Chymique"</note> extracts it easily, nevertheless I wish to give this particular advice: one must never pulverize the **aromatics** <note>Fragrant plant materials, such as spices.</note> to distill them (as some do), but rather they should only be broken or put in **sticks** <note>original: "lingots"; here referring to the natural quill shape of cinnamon bark rather than metal bars.</note>; for by this means one obtains more oil—a thing I have well experienced.

### Another method to obtain even more oil than by the ordinary way of distilling.

Having broken the cinnamon (I mean choice cinnamon, or whatever other aromatic it may be), place it in the **retort** <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-curving neck used for distilling liquids.</note>, distilling it in a **vapor bath** <note>original: "bain vaporeux"; a method of indirect heating using steam, similar to a double boiler, to ensure a gentle and even temperature.</note>, and the water shall come forth together with the oil. Once the distillation is done, pour the water back over fresh cinnamon wood and re-distill it, continuing this several times; and in this manner you shall have a good quantity of water and oil. As for the **dregs** <note>original: "feces"; the solid residue remaining in the vessel after the spirit and oil have been extracted.</note> at the bottom, they will be so black and dry that they will resemble charcoal.

### Its virtues and uses.

This oil comforts all the principal members of the body, and especially the cold **stomach** <note>original: "ventricule"; in early modern medicine, this term specifically referred to the stomach. A "cold" stomach was believed to cause indigestion and sluggishness.</note>, the heart, and the brain; it dispels the

### *Comforting balms made solid by means of wax.*

Inasmuch as aromatic oils, being liquid, cannot be carried for fear of spilling or the breaking of the glass vial, the Chemists have invented a very secure way to be able to carry them more conveniently, whether in boxes of pewter <note>original: "estain plomb"; a lead-tin alloy commonly used for small containers.</note>, silver, or tinplate <note>original: "fer blanc"; literally "white iron," which is sheet iron coated with tin to prevent rusting.</note>.

Now, to make them, it will be enough to have provided this satisfaction to the curious: the best method is to add white wax that has been boiled in rose water.

The usual application is to the nostrils, the temples, the neck, and the stomach.

### *Mitigating and sleep-inducing anodynes.*

There are many illnesses which cannot be cured without anodynes <note>From the Greek *an-odynos*, meaning "without pain." These are substances used to lessen or eliminate physical suffering.</note>; therefore, in all treatments of diseases which cause great pain, one can use internal and appropriate anodynes, so that rest—the friend of nature—may be restored once the pernicious roots of the symptoms have been driven out.

In matters of medicine, sleep is a secret surpassing all the powers of precious stones; and he who can conveniently apply a sleep-inducer <note>original: "dormitoire"; here referring to a medicinal preparation intended to provoke sleep rather than a sleeping chamber.</note>, drawn from a true essence, deserves to be called a good Physician, especially when those diseases that are enemies of sleep repeatedly wake the resting patient.

## *Observations on the preparation of Laudanum.*

<margin>Then the greatest strength and primary substance of the spirit of the herb is still as if concentrated there.</margin>
Take the roots and bark of young and fresh henbane <note>A toxic plant in the nightshade family, used as a powerful sedative</note> (having removed the central core) gathered when the Sun and the Moon are in the sign of Aries, or of Libra, and this must be before the Moon is at its full: there are some who gather them at the same hour and moment that the Moon enters these signs. This expressed juice, skimmed and filtered, being placed in a warm place, thickens like honey, and hardens in the Sun: from the said juice, one can draw the tincture with spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol used as a solvent</note>.

One must purge the opium in a liquor of hyssop <note>A medicinal plant used for cleansing</note>, or distilled water, as one is accustomed to do with aloes, which must then be drawn out with spirit of wine.

The juice of henbane and the opium must have cast off their sulphur <note>In alchemy, "sulphur" refers to the oily, combustible principle of a substance, often believed to carry its "venomous" or toxic qualities</note> and harmful venom before being mixed with the others; and it is this which rises to the surface in the form of foam; for if the opium and henbane are not cleansed and purified of their poisonous sulphur, they will cause a great diversity of symptoms: a thing which has not yet been noticed by any other person; which is the reason why I wanted to give warning of it, so that you might take care.

### *Electuary of Laudanum.*

### *The powers and usage of the Electuary of Laudanum.*

This Laudanum in the form of an electuary <term>Electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term> is a medicine that deserves to bear the name of *Laudanum* <note>derived from the Latin 'laudare', to praise; Crollius suggests the medicine is "praiseworthy"</note>, seeing as it corresponds to it entirely.

### *The dose.*

The dose is from two to four grains <note>A "grain" was a tiny unit of weight based on a single grain of wheat, approximately 65 milligrams</note>. If the bowels are free <note>meaning if the patient is not constipated</note>, then it is more effective in demonstrating the effects of its strength and virtue. It is also given with appropriate and specific waters, mixed with them according to the seven principal members <note>In Renaissance medicine, these were the vital organs believed to govern the body: the brain, heart, liver, lungs, stomach, kidneys, and the "vital spirit" (or sometimes the spleen or genitals)</note>, or the nature of the illness; but if the illness is severe, one can make a pill from it and give it around nighttime, provided the patient has eaten some time before; at midnight one can give another, and in the morning a third, and by this means health is restored.

## Oil of Amber.

To make and prepare the oil of Amber <note>original: "Succin". Amber was a prized substance in early modern pharmacy, believed to have powerful effects on the nervous system.</note>, great diligence is needed, as it requires a suitable and proportionate fire. We are accustomed to using white Amber generated from the purest bitumen of the sea <note>In the 17th century, the origin of amber was debated; many believed it was a mineral bitumen that hardened in the ocean rather than fossilized tree resin.</note>; yellow amber is also found, which we reject for medicinal use in this case.

Now, to do it well, one must first have white Amber coarsely crushed, and washed in common water (if necessity requires it) two or three pounds, which must afterwards be put into the cucurbit <note>original: "courle". The bottom part of a still, usually gourd-shaped.</note> or alembic that is not very tall; therein you shall pour a good quantity of rose water and betony water; (these two waters are put there so that the oil does not burn, and so that by their means the distillation begins more easily). On the body of the alembic, place and add the appropriate head <note>original: "chapiteau". The "cap" or top part of the still where vapors condense before flowing down the beak.</note>, which should have a beak as long as you can find, and appropriately wide. Adapt your receiver <term>Receiver: The "recipient" or vessel placed at the end of the still's beak to collect the distilled product.</term> to the end of the beak, and perform your distillation in a sand bath <term>Sand bath: Also called "distillation au sable," this involves placing the glass vessel in a tray of sand to distribute heat evenly and prevent the glass from shattering over a direct flame.</term>, the joints being well luted <note>original: "lutées". Sealed with "lute," a paste made of clay, dung, or flour used to make the apparatus airtight.</note> according to the custom of the art. One must nevertheless watch the degrees of fire, for fear that the glass might blacken, for it would become like charcoal and immediately break; care must also be taken not to force the fire too much, for the receiver would be in danger by this means.

In this distillation, the water comes out first, and afterwards follows the white oil with the spirit, similar

The ordinary dose of oil of Amber is four, six, seven, up to ten drops; even as much as one scruple <note>An apothecary unit of weight equal to 1/3 of a drachm, roughly 1.3 grams or 20 grains.</note>, depending on the illness and the constitution <note>original: "complexion"; in the 17th century, this referred to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) in an individual.</note> of the patient.

### *The powers, use, and dosage of milk of sulfur.*

It is the balm of the radical moisture <note>original: "l'humide radical," the vital fluid believed by early physicians to sustain life and bodily heat</note>.
It strengthens the natural forces.
It purges the blood of all its impurities, from which diseases are accustomed to take their origin.
It is an admirable preventative against apoplexy <note>a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>, and against contractions of the nerves.
It works wonders against leprosy, and the great pox <note>original: "la verolle," usually referring to syphilis</note>.
It is a specific remedy for the lungs, also preventing and curing asthma.
It cures coughs, both long-standing and recent, and comforts the brain.
It consumes and dries out the discharges <note>original: "defluxions," the flowing of excess humors, often manifesting as mucus or catarrh</note> from the head.

It prevents and expels gases from the stomach <note>original: "ventriculle"</note>, and likewise treats colic.

It greatly benefits those who are dry, withered, and suffering from hectic fevers <note>wasting illnesses or chronic fevers</note> when mixed with cinnamon water and prepared as a milk.

It visibly relieves those with consumption <note>original: "phthifiques"; sufferers of tuberculosis or similar wasting lung diseases</note>, insofar as it acts to preserve the radical moisture <term>Radical moisture: The innate, vital fluid believed by early physicians to be the fuel for the body's internal heat and life; its exhaustion was thought to cause aging and death</term>, as those who have used it can well testify.

It is wonderful for gout <note>specifically "podagra," or gout of the foot</note>, for sciatica, and other similar ailments.

It secretly consumes the disease no differently than fire consumes wood.

### *The dosage of the milk of sulfur.*

One must put this milk <note>A white, milky precipitate of sulfur</note> or powder into cinnamon water, lemon balm, or lavender water; in epileptic water <note>a distilled remedy intended to treat seizures</note>, or spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note>.

One adds only a tiny amount to the aforementioned waters until they become whitish; then, one takes a spoonful of the mixed water morning and evening.

Note that the mixing should only be done shortly before one intends to take it.

And if by some artifice these spirits could be put in a position to perform their functions, and extricate themselves...

<margin>Gold is the governor of all other things; indeed, it is the receptacle of all celestial virtues, for the quintessence <note>The "fifth essence" or purest, most concentrated part of a substance</note> of gold resists the operation of the Sun and the other Planets when it is given to man.</margin>

<margin>Four natural principles</margin>
Thrice and four times blessed is the Physician who, through a physical rotation <note>original: "roulement"; likely referring to the circulatory distillation processes in the alchemical vessel</note>, can reduce the three universal principles <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—the foundational elements of matter in Paracelsian chemistry</note>, well-purified and joined in due proportion, into an incombustible phoenix <note>A symbol for the Philosopher's Stone, which survives the fire and grants rebirth</note>. By the benefit of this phoenix, he can animate gold and make it vegetative <note>Able to grow and multiply its medicinal power</note>; and by the same means of a sort of indissoluble bond, turn his phoenix into gold. This physician, favored by the celestial Sun and through the Laws of Anatomy, Magic, Philosophy, and Pyronomy <term>Pyronomy: The art or science of regulating fire for chemical operations</term>, knows how to apply the spirit of life to the Microcosmic heart (that is, the heart of man, as there is a sympathy between them). He does this by means of the metallic Sun <note>Philosophical gold</note>, dissolved and regenerated by the "water of many names," or hyleal water <term>Hyleal water: From 'hyle' (matter); the primordial, chaotic source-liquid of the alchemists</term>, guided by the appropriate spirit of wine <note>Highly distilled alcohol used as a solvent for medicines</note>.

<margin>Among celestial things, the Sun holds the first rank. Among plants, wine. Among animals, the heart. Among metals, gold.</margin>
But since the Sovereign Giver of perfections has not yet wished to cast His eye upon me (as I have said before), even though I have made the attempt in several ways and at my own expense with "potable gold"—or more accurately, "pitiful gold" <note>original: "putable." # OF CROLLIUS #

<margin>
The Sun always shines and borrows its light from no one, being governed by God alone. It is impossible to accomplish anything without the favor of the Moon, seeing that the Moon is (by the power of the Sun) the lady and mistress of generation, of growth, and of decay. One shines as if by another’s light, because she does not shine by herself but borrows all her splendor from the Sun. Without the favor of the Moon, we cannot in any way whatsoever attract the force of the celestial influences.
</margin>

The Sun has been destined by Divine power to ignite all the other fires, namely the spheres of the Planets, which we cannot discern; for of themselves they are as if dead, yet by the blazing of the Sun—which gives them the power to operate each according to its own faculties—they are vivified.

The Sun is also called the <term>Spiracle of life</term> <note>From the Latin *spiraculum*, meaning a breathing hole or vent; here it refers to the Sun as the "breath" that sustains the life of the elements.</note> of the elements: by **Paracelsus, Plato, and Zoroaster**, it is called **Celestial and invincible Fire**; the father of light, who communicates his splendor to all the other celestial bodies, and from there, by a certain hidden <note>The original French uses *vertu occulte*, referring to the "hidden power" or natural magnetism believed to exist in all things.</note> virtue, derives it into our own fire; and in this way, the virtues of all the other Planets are found again within the Sun. 

This is why **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and the divine nature of the cosmos.</note> says that all the gifts we possess come from the Sun, either mediately or immediately: for the other virtues communicated to us from the other Planets are held only as if by a loan, seeing as they possess them only through communication. Thus it follows that in the Sun—the heart of heaven—all hidden virtues reveal themselves as if from a most powerful source. But the Moon, the wife of the Sun and the final receptacle of all celestial virtues and influences, attracts into her womb (as it were) all the rays and influences of the Sun and other Planets; these she brings forth and communicates to this lower world, her closest neighbor. And it is to be judged that Almighty God created and placed the Moon at the lowest point of the celestial spheres and bodies, and at the highest point of the elements, so that the influences and forces of the stars might more conveniently be communicated by her means to the elements.

superior [bodies], and by a certain proportion from degree to degree, down to the globe of the earth, rendering to each body the properties of the star which predominates in their nature and essence. And from this it appears how the <term>Soul of the World</term> <note>Often referred to as the *Anima Mundi*, this was believed to be an intrinsic connection between all living things on Earth and the spiritual realm.</note> disposes of the light and fire of the Sun, through another fire which is invisible and insensible—I mean the [spiritual] Sun which afterwards moves the virtues of the stars, and finally causes them to flow down here by the favor of the Moon, in the same way as the seed of man when it is driven into the womb of the woman.

Now then, since the celestial Sun and the terrestrial Sun, which is gold, have between them this singular concordance and resemblance, it is not without reason that the wise <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Here referring to Hermetic or alchemical philosophers who studied the mystical properties of symbols and names.</note> wished to signify them by one and the same character <note>A "character" in this context is a symbolic glyph or alchemical shorthand.</note>, namely by a round or whole circle having a visible center, of which here is the figure: <image-desc>alchemical symbol for the sun: a circle with a dot in the center</image-desc>; for thus the character of the Sun demonstrates both heaven and earth; the circle shows the celestial movements and influences; the point which is its center shows the terrestrial and fixed nature. And whoever has the true science of the point and center can say that there is nothing in nature of which he does not have perfect knowledge. For since the root and foundation of all occult <note>In the 17th century, "occult" simply meant "hidden" or "not immediately visible to the senses."</note> things consists in the point, it is beyond doubt that the foundation of all arts and natural sciences cannot be drawn from anywhere else. But, let us return to our <term>potable gold</term> <note>From the Latin *aurum potabile*; a legendary alchemical medicine consisting of gold dissolved in a liquid state, thought to cure all diseases and grant longevity.</note> which was communicated to me, and which I wish to teach after my own.

## THE LIME OF THE SUN.

*Take half a pound of common <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: *eau forte*; literally "strong water," referring to nitric acid.</note>, in which you will dissolve one ounce of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: *sel Armoniac*; ammonium chloride, used here to transform the acid.</note>, or as much as can be dissolved therein; make your solution with a gentle heat, and by this means you will have <term>aqua regia</term> <note>original: *eau regalle*; "royal water," a mixture of acids capable of dissolving the "king" of metals, gold.</note>, in which you will dissolve as much gold as shall be necessary. Afterward, you will place your solution in a sufficiently large glass vessel, pouring into it gently and drop by drop some good <term>oil of Tartar</term> <note>original: *huille de tartre*; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, which acts as a base.</note>, which has dissolved by itself in the coolness of a cellar. I say gently and drop by drop because of the danger of <term>ebullition</term> <note>boiling over or violent bubbling caused by the chemical reaction.</note>; or in the absence of this oil of Tartar, you may use common salt, dissolved in common water. It is nevertheless necessary to have a good quantity of oil of Tartar, if you wish for the gold to immediately sink to the bottom by <term>precipitation</term> <note>original: *repercussion*; the process where a solid is forced out of a liquid solution.</note>: and as soon as you see that all the lime of the dissolved gold is at the bottom (which you will easily recognize by the color of the water, which ought to be white; for if it is yellowish, it is a sign that all the gold has not yet been precipitated to the bottom), you shall throw in more oil of Tartar; be warned of this in passing, and at my own expense <note>A common alchemical phrase meaning the author learned this through his own costly trial and error.</note>. # OF CROLLIUS #

->A I<-

One or two grains placed upon a knife or other iron blade, with a candle held beneath, produces as loud a noise as a <term>petard</term> <note>A small bomb or firecracker used to blow open gates or walls.</note>, no matter how large it may be; indeed, this sound is so sharp that it nearly wounds the hearing of those who listen to it. The operation of this powder is contrary to that of **gunpowder**; for while gunpowder typically expands outward, this gold powder, when placed upon an iron blade and set on fire, pierces it, recoiling downwards even though the metal be quite thick. I believe that the cause of this percussion is **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sel armoniac*; ammonium chloride, which Crollius believes provides the "spirit" for the explosion.</note>. I shall set down my reasons here until someone provides me with better ones: for just as **saltpeter** <note>original: *sel nitre*</note> and **sulfur** are enemies and cannot endure one another—which is clearly seen as soon as fire takes hold—likewise **sal ammoniac** and **Tartar** cannot agree. Now, when sal ammoniac is joined with its enemy **oil of Tartar** <note>original: *huille de Tartre*; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate.</note>, it results in a greater struggle, during which the gold—which had previously been dissolved in this **aqua regia** <note>original: *eau regalle*; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids, the only solvent known to dissolve gold.</note>—falls out of the solution. The oil of Tartar struggles with the greatly purified spirit of the ammoniac; in the midst of this struggle, it joins with its adversary, the **sulfur of the Sun** <note>original: *soulphre du Soleil*; in alchemical theory, gold is composed of a perfectly purified "sulfur" and "mercury."</note>. And because this sulfur of the Sun is exceptionally well-purified by nature, and much more subtle than our common sulfur, it is not without reason that it operates with greater efficacy and in smaller quantities.

### *The powers and usage of this oil of Vitriol*

**Paracelsus** calls it the **fourth part of the Pharmacopoeia** <note>A formal collection or book of medicinal recipes.</note>, and advises every pharmacist to keep it in his shop as its **cornerstone**.

For all **headaches**, from whatever cause they might arise, it should be taken in lily water—which the Latins call *Juno’s Rose* <note>original: "Rosa Iunonis." For the **plague**, it must be mixed with sugar candy and an **electuary** <note>A medicinal paste or syrup made by mixing powders with honey or sugar.</note> of juniper.

Those who are tormented by the application of **mercury** <note>Mercury was a standard but highly toxic treatment for "the Great Pox" (syphilis); the "torment" refers to the severe side effects of mercury poisoning.</note> can use it mixed with **Theriac** <note>A legendary polypharmaceutical "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, used since antiquity.</note>, and they shall be cured through sweating.

No one can recover their health without pain, just as the pregnant woman is never in a good state until she has felt the pangs of childbirth.

It cures all kinds of **tetters** <note>original: "dertres"; a general term for various skin eruptions like eczema or psoriasis.</note>, scabs, itching, and everything that tends to cling to the skin, such as severe scald-head <note>original: "male-tigne"</note>, **skin-mites** <note>original: "syrons"; likely referring to the mites that cause scabies.</note>, etc. However, the ointment must be applied without pity, for the patient must not be spared at all <note>This warning reflects the caustic, burning nature of the concentrated acid oil when applied to the skin.</note>.

One can use it after being purged with appropriate waters, and it is useful in almost every kind of illness, for it defends against and prevents all **putrefaction** <note>In early medicine, many diseases were believed to be caused by the "rotting" or corruption of the body's internal fluids.</note> through its acidity, besides the fact that it clears away obstructions.

->*The dosage of the said oil of vitriol.*<-

This oil has a rather tart taste, and is administered in **specific waters** <note>Distilled herbal waters intended for a particular ailment.</note>; regarding the quantity, it is given until one feels, upon putting it to the mouth, that it might set the teeth on edge.

It must not be taken alone, but always with a **vehicle** <term>original: "viatique"; in medical chemistry, a liquid carrier used to administer a potent medicine, such as wine, broth, or herbal water.</term>; this was not understood by a certain chemist (whom I do not wish to name), who, thinking he was doing a great favor for one of his friends, snatched away not only the illness, but his life as well, for having given him too large a quantity. Therefore, one must use it with prudence and stir it vigorously and firmly when one wishes to use it, for it sinks straight to the bottom because of its weight; let the dosage, then, be according to your judgment and prudence.

### ADVISORIES.

Because of its **acrimony** <note>Its sharp, biting, or corrosive quality.</note>, it benefits the languid **stomach** <term>original: "ventriculle"; the physical organ of digestion.</term> (provided, however, that there is no **choler** <note>Here referring to an excess of yellow bile or an inflammatory "hot" condition.</note> or **abscess** <term>original: "aposteme"; a localized collection of pus or a painful swelling.</term> therein). In fact, those of **bilious** and **choleric** <note>In the ancient system of the four humors, "choleric" individuals were thought to be hot and dry by nature, making them sensitive to sharp or acidic medicines.</note> temperaments must abstain from it because of the harm it would bring them; for the mixture of **black bile** or **atrabile** <term>The humor associated with melancholy; literally "dark bile."</term> with this oil would cause nothing but great **effervescences** <note>original: "ebullitions"; a chemical reaction where the liquid appears to boil or bubble violently.</note>, no more and no less than **oil of tartar** <note>Potassium carbonate in liquid form.</note> and **aqua fortis** <note>Nitric acid. Mixing these substances creates a vigorous chemical reaction.</note>.

Now then, he who wishes to use it with the proper vehicle must take it warm, and afterward keep himself in bed, and allow...

### *A Uterine Remedy for the stomach.* <note>The original term "ventriculle" usually refers to the stomach, but in this context of "uterine" health, it relates to the belief that the womb could affect the digestive organs or "rise" within the body.</note>

### *Elixir for the belly.*

### *Observations.*

For the **provocation of the months** <note>original: "prouocation des mois"; the induction of the menstrual cycle, which was often suppressed in various illnesses.</note>, one must take care to observe the time they were accustomed to come to the sick person, for it is then that pains of the kidneys <note>original: "reins"; in this period, this often refers generally to the lower back area.</note> and the flanks never fail to arrive; it is therefore at that time that the medicine must be given, for with the assistance of nature, one is assured of recovering entire and perfect health.

## *Salt of Jupiter.*

<note>In the symbolic language of alchemy, "Jupiter" refers to the metal **Tin**. "Salt of Jupiter" is a chemical salt derived from tin, often used in early modern medicine for its perceived cooling and stabilizing properties.</note>

Take **ashes of Jupiter** <insert>calx of tin</insert> prepared by open fire without any **sophistication** <term>original: "sophistication"; the common practice of adulterating or diluting a chemical substance with inferior materials.</term>, from which you will draw the salt in distilled vinegar, and afterwards sweeten it with distilled rainwater, filtering and evaporating it slowly in the **bath** <note>original: "au bain"; referring to a *balneum Mariae* or water bath, which allows for gentle, indirect heating.</note> about seven different times, or thereabouts.

### *The powers and usage with the dose of the Salt of Jupiter.*

It is a most admirable secret for the **suffocation of the womb** <note>original: "suffocation de matrice"; a historical medical condition also known as hysteria, where the womb was thought to wander or rise in the body, causing respiratory distress. It was often treated with strong-smelling or temperature-altering substances to "drive" the organ back to its place.</note> by rubbing the navel warmly with this salt, for as soon as the womb feels the heat, it returns to its place and moves no more.

### *The dose of the said salt.*

The dose is the weight of three **grains** <term>A minute unit of weight based on the mass of a single seed of cereal; approximately 65 milligrams.</term> during three or four consecutive mornings, in **Mugwort water** <note>original: "eau d'Artemise"; a herbal distillate of *Artemisia vulgaris*, traditionally used to regulate menstruation.</note> or another **cordial water** <note>A medicinal drink intended to stimulate the heart or improve the patient's "spirits" and vitality.</note>.

### *The Dose.*

To robust individuals, one should give one dram <note>Approximately 3.9 grams.</note>, but for the young and the weak, one must be content with half a dram, for that is enough to cure the illness.

Those who wish to use it as a preventative are accustomed to taking only eight or ten grains <note>A very small unit of weight; 1 dram equals 60 grains.</note>.

One can also make lozenges from them, mixed with sugar, gum tragacanth <note>A natural gum obtained from the dried sap of several species of Middle Eastern legumes, used as a binder.</note>, and pectoral water <note>A medicinal water intended to treat ailments of the chest and lungs.</note>.

Care must be taken not to give any (no more than the oil <note>Referring to the oil of sulfur mentioned in previous sections.</note>) to pregnant women, for they immediately provoke the menses <note>original: "prouoquent les mois"; substances that "provoke the months" were emmenagogues, which could induce miscarriage and were thus strictly forbidden during pregnancy.</note>.

### *Its virtues & uses with the dose.*

One uses this with admiration for the plague, provided that the patient takes a spoonful of it every twelve hours in good wine: and that they endure the sweating for three hours, and that they do not eat for six hours after taking the potion.

It purges the head, the chest, and all the principal organs of the body, greatly strengthening them, expelling and healing the ulcers that might be found there; and indeed, having healed them, it prevents them from being so easily re-injured.

This water also brings relief to those who have been rubbed with Mercury <note>Mercury "rubbing" or inunction was the standard treatment for syphilis, but it often led to severe poisoning; this remedy was intended to "expel" the toxic mercury from the patient's system.</note>, for by a singular virtue it penetrates the nerves, muscles, and even into the marrow of the bones, correcting and driving out everything it encounters...

### *Podagric <note>original: "Podagrique"; relating to gout, specifically in the feet.</note> or remedy for the gout.*

The gout or podagra <note>original: "poudagre"; a term derived from the Greek *pous* (foot) and *agra* (seizure).</note>, according to the opinion of Petrus Severinus <note>original: "P.Seuerin"; Petrus Severinus (1542–1602) was a Danish physician and an influential follower of Paracelsus.</note>, can be cured at its onset by a single ointment, or balm, insofar as it allows for the mixing of resolvents <note>original: "resolutifs"; medicines used to disperse or "resolve" inflammatory humors.</note>, mitigatives <note>original: "mitigatifs"; substances that soothe or ease pain.</note>, and corroboratives <note>original: "corroboratifs"; agents used to strengthen the limbs or organs.</note>.

Confirmed and long-standing gout, which has planted its roots—which are difficult to resolve—in the blood, or in the flesh, or even in the synovia <note>original: "synouie"; the lubricating fluid found in the joints.</note> itself; cannot be cured with external balms, mitigatives, resolvents, and corroboratives alone-

Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician who pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> maintains that three things are required for the cure of gout: namely, resolutives, mitigatives, and corroboratives.

For the mitigative <note>original: "mitigatif"; a substance used to soothe pain and reduce inflammation.</note>, one should make use of these two following balms.

Among the corroboratives <note>original: "corroboratifs"; strengthening agents intended to prevent the return of the illness.</note> that prevent the defluxion, one must not forget the spirit of vitriol <note>original: "efprit de vitriol"; sulfuric acid, often used in highly diluted forms in alchemical medicine.</note>, along with the salt of pearls, and the wine of Cloves <note>original: "Geroffle"</note> and of Acorus <note>original: "Acorus"; sweet flag, an aromatic root.</note> of Paracelsus; inasmuch as it dries and prevents defluxions.

### First gout balsam.

<margin>Take</margin>
- Two pounds of vitriol <term>vitriol: a sulfate of iron or copper, common in alchemy</term> calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove moisture or impurities</note> until it turns yellow.
- One pound of virgin honey with the honeycomb.
- One pound of spirit of wine <note>distilled alcohol</note>; if one can obtain some that has been prepared with the composition of Laudanum <note>an opium-based tincture</note>, it will be the best.
- Four ounces of turpentine.
- Four ounces of rosemary.
- Six ounces of vervain of each <note>original: "ana"; a Latin medical term meaning 'equal parts of each'</note>.
- Half a pound of calcined pebble <note>likely flint or quartz, heated until brittle and powdered</note>.

Everything must be ground together and placed in a glazed alembic <note>a chemical vessel used for distillation</note> that is well-luted <note>original: "luté"; sealed with 'lute,' a paste made of clay or resin to ensure the vessel is airtight</note>, which should have a large head and a sufficiently large receiver vessel, the joints of which are also to be sealed. Place your alembic for three days to digest <note>a process of slow, gentle heating to extract essences</note> in a gentle sand-bath fire; after that time has passed, it must be distilled little by little, observing the various degrees of heat, then strengthening the fire at the end. During the time you see the drops or "spirit" emerging, let it cool afterward, and reverberate <note>subject to intense heat in a furnace</note> the "dead mass" or dregs <note>original: "feces"; the solid remains left after distillation</note>, which are spongy and black, until they become white. Then, pouring the first liquid back onto them, you shall distill them for a second time.

## *Nephritic.* <note>Nephritic refers to diseases of the kidneys, particularly the formation of stones</note>

There are various kinds of calculus <term>calculus: a stone or solid mass formed in the body, such as a kidney stone</term>, of which the degrees and parts are different in number; all of these, nevertheless, are produced from the most impure portion of food, refined and destined for coagulation <note>In this period, digestion was seen as a chemical process of separating "pure" nutrients from "impure" waste</note>, after the separation of the more benign nourishment, performed by the benefit of the spirit, or the heat of the [internal] parts. These degrees of calculus are shaped differently because of the variety of materials from which they originate, and the multiplicity of the parts to which they become adherent; for they give to each part associated symptoms through the great affinity they have together.

<margin>If the expulsive force is weak, then the coagulative force of the salt creates tartar.</margin>
Strong digestion performs a sudden operation upon the calculus; for a thin, delicate person of small complexion, who can only digest with difficulty, is never likely to be subject to the calculus, unless the weak digestion is expelled by the strength of the expulsive faculties without separation <note>Meaning the waste is moved through the body before it has a chance to settle and "coagulate" into a stone</note>; for then it is impossible that the man be without tartar <term>tartar: in Paracelsian medicine, "tartar" refers to any stony or gravel-like deposit that "precipitates" out of body fluids, similar to how tartar forms in wine barrels</term>, which (coagulated) by the spirit of salt <term>spirit of salt: a chemical principle related to solidification and preservation; not necessarily modern hydrochloric acid in this context</term> cannot be dissolved by any purgation whatsoever.

One must take care not to give any sharp or stinging medicines to those who are subject to the calculus.
