### *Salt against the calculus.* <note>Calculus refers to kidney or bladder stones.</note>

**P**aracelsus says that there is no assurance for the stone in the length of remedies, but rather in the true preparation of them.

Take then:

*   Crayfish eyes <term>Crayfish eyes: also called gastroliths, these are calcium deposits found in the stomachs of crayfish used as a source of calcium carbonate</term>.
*   Human stone or gravel <note>In the medical tradition of the time, actual kidney or bladder stones were sometimes processed and used as a remedy for the same condition, following the principle of "like cures like."</note>
*   Judaic stone <term>Judaic stone: Lapis Judaicus, fossilized spines of ancient sea urchins, traditionally used for urinary ailments</term>.
*   Lynx stone <term>Lynx stone: Lapis Lyncis; historically believed to be petrified lynx urine, though usually fossilized belemnites</term>.
*   Sponge stone <note>Lapis Spongiae, small stony concretions found within sea sponges.</note>
*   Eagle stone <note>original: "Pierre aquillée," referring to the Aetites, a hollow stone containing another stone inside, often used in folk and chemical medicine.</note>
*   Crystal.
*   Pebble [Flint].
*   Stones from the fish called Perch <term>Perch stones: the otoliths or ear-stones found in the heads of perch fish, used for their high calcium content</term>.

All of these you shall dissolve with distilled vinegar, repeating the pouring until everything is entirely dissolved. From this, prepare the salt by drawing off the vinegar. Use the salt on its own, or if you wish, dissolve it with some liquor; however, only after you have frequently purified or sweetened <term>dulcify: to wash a substance with water to remove acidic or salty residues</term> it with rain water, which you will evaporate through a filter immediately afterward.

### *The virtues, uses, and dose of the salt.*

This salt is marvelous for every kind of stone, in whatever part of the body it may be.

The dose is one to two scruples <term>Scruple: a traditional unit of weight used by apothecaries, roughly equal to 1.3 grams</term> for those who only fear being afflicted by it, and they should take it at every quarter of the moon <note>Astrological timing was considered essential for the efficacy of chemical medicines.</note> in a suitable syrup.

Those who are already afflicted with the stone must take from two scruples up to one dram <term>Dram: or drachm, an apothecary weight equal to three scruples (approx. 3.9 grams)</term> for their health, along with specific herbal waters such as rest-harrow <note>original: "Arreste-bœuf," a plant named for its tough roots that could "stop an ox" pulling a plow; it was traditionally used as a diuretic</note>, saxifrage, burnet, or parsley.

To women, it should be given in balm water or juniper water.

## Two observations.

Note that to make this salt volatile—meaning flighty or light—it must be dissolved often, and toward the end, digested with good spirit of wine <term>Spirit of wine: a highly distilled alcohol, similar to modern ethanol, used as a solvent in alchemy</term>, and then removed over hot ashes by evaporation. This is because, after any kind of putrefaction <note>In alchemy, putrefaction refers to the breakdown or fermentation of a substance to release its "inner" virtues</note>, half an ounce of salt rises. As for the essence of wine, according to the opinion of Paracelsus, it should in no way be separated from the flying or volatile salt; this is so that it may act more powerfully upon the internal tartar <term>Internal tartar: metabolic waste or mineral buildup that Paracelsus believed caused stones and joint pain</term>. For when the spirit of wine is fermented with the power of the aforementioned stones, it has more strength to dissolve a person's calculus, in the same way that alcohol of wine fortified with tartar prevents one from being able to remove the color from gold or corals.

<margin>
A very unique
powder
for the stone.
</margin>
No one should be surprised that it is necessary to calcine <term>Calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures in order to reduce it to a powder</term> the stones of crystal, flint, Lapis Judaicus <note>original: "Judaïque"; fossilized sea urchin spines used since antiquity to treat kidney stones</note>, Lynx stone <note>original: "de Lynx"; fossilized prehistoric squid shells, also called belemnites</note>, sponge stone, and Eagle stone <note>original: "d’Aigle"; hollow geodes thought to have medicinal and protective properties</note> with saltpeter. This is done so that they may more easily be dissolved with the aforementioned vinegar; otherwise, they would be insoluble. Furthermore, crude saltpeter purified by sulfur, with a little saffron, Mace <note>The spice derived from the reddish shell of the nutmeg seed</note>, and Citrine stones <note>yellow-colored quartz or crystals</note>, is a very effective remedy for the stone.

### *Dysentery.*

If digestion is good, but does not produce a separation <note>In early modern medicine, "separation" refers to the body's ability to distinguish and sort nutritious "juice" from waste</note>, one is certain to be afflicted with dysentery; but if the separation occurs without digestion, it is then only lientery <term>Lientery: a form of diarrhea where food passes through the body in a nearly undigested state</term>.

But if, by chance, neither separation nor digestion is observed, one can say with certainty that diarrhea has formed; as for the "flux of the belly," the signs are clear and manifest by the putrefaction of the matter, which varies in color.

### Essence of Saffron of Mars.

Take yellow rust of iron; the best is found in Nuremberg; choose that which appears to be glazed; you will find it in iron foundries or at forge hammers <term>Martinets: large, water-powered tilt hammers used in forges to shape iron</term>.

Once the period of fourteen days has expired, it must be filtered, and the vinegar removed in a water bath <note>original: "au bain," referring to a bain-marie</note>; the red matter remains at the bottom, but it must be recovered with rainwater to remove its sour taste. After this calcination, it should be sweetened again with common water. If this is done properly as it should be, it will dissolve into an oil by itself—if not entirely, at least in part—when ground upon marble in a very damp place.

### *The Dosage.*

The dose is from half a <term>drachm: an ancient unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce</term> to a full drachm, in a glass of <term>Malvasia: a sweet, aromatic Mediterranean wine highly prized in the Renaissance</term>, or other good wine.

One cannot have the wheat without the tares <note>original: "l'yuroye"; darnel or weeds that grow among grain</note>, nor honey without the sting.
</margin>

The strength and efficacy of this medicine will never astonish those who know that the ordinary nature of poisons is to contain within themselves their own remedy. And because bad things can naturally remain joined with the good, for this reason many people eat the flesh of vipers without horror or any danger, knowing that it will prolong their life. It is not, therefore, without reason that <term>Baldus Angellus: Baldo Angelo Abati, a 16th-century Italian physician famous for his work on the medicinal properties of vipers</term> maintains this discourse, which I have inserted in his own words from the book he wrote on *the admirable nature of vipers* <note>original Latin: "admirabili viperarum natura"</note>. These are his words: 

"One thing comes to my mind as intensely wonderful: that by the serpent's cunning, death entered into the world; it is also marvelous that from the death of the viper serpent, and from its flesh, one is cured of all the more serious diseases and poisons, and restored to one’s former state; indeed, by the continued use of viper flesh, one is preserved from all diseases; this certainly surpasses and exceeds all wonder." <note>original Latin: "Illud vnum venit mihi in mentem vehementer admirandum, serpentis astu in orbem terrarum mortem intrasse; illud etiam mirum ex vipera serpentis nece, & eius carne ab omnibus grauioribus morbis atque venenis curari, & in pristinum restitui, sed continuato viperina carnis vsu, ab omnibus morbis præseruari; hoc certè totum omnem admirationem superat & excedit."</note>

### *Its virtues, and uses.*

For every kind of wound, one must make a small medicinal pad <term>Plumaceau: a soft pad or pledget of lint or cotton used in dressing wounds</term> of cotton, or of the down that grows around blessed thistle, or on poplars; having made this pad, dip it in the said balm, and place it slightly warm upon the wound (note that every wound should have been washed with wine). Over the pad, one must apply an astringent plaster <note>A medical dressing designed to contract tissues and stop bleeding</note>, and leave it there.

### *Stictic, or Astringent, Plaster.*

In the composition of any stictic <term>Stictic: From the Latin "sticticum," a term popularized by Paracelsus for a plaster that "fixes" or heals wounds by drawing the edges together.</term> plaster whatsoever, <term>Paracelsus</term> <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), known as Paracelsus, was a Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine by using minerals and chemicals rather than just herbs.</note> says that four different types of ingredients must be considered.

First, the healing which is achieved by means of wax and rosin <note>original: "poix raisine," a resinous substance derived from pine used to give plasters their stickiness.</note>.

Secondly, the complications <note>original: "accidents," referring to secondary medical symptoms or side effects.</note> which are removed and prevented by the benefit of gums; namely, <term>Galbanum</term>, <term>Opopanax</term>, <term>Sagapenum</term> <note>OCR: "Sapag."</note>, <term>Bdellium</term> <note>OCR: "Bdell."</note>, <term>Ammoniacum</term>, and <term>Elemi</term> <note>These are all aromatic resins gathered from various plants, traditionally used in pharmacy for their adhesive, warming, and "drawing" qualities.</note>.

Thirdly, one must consider putrefaction (since any wound whatsoever is naturally inclined toward rot, generating worms or the growth of "proud flesh" <note>original: "mauvaise chair," referring to unhealthy or excessive tissue growth that hinders healing.</note>;) now, this putrefaction is removed and prevented by the power of consolidants <term>Consolidants: Remedies believed to "consolidate" or knit the flesh and bone back together.</term>, namely <term>Mastic</term>, <term>Myrrh</term>, and the like.

### *Sugar, Salt, Butter, or Honey of Saturn.*
<note>In alchemy, Saturn is the symbolic name for the metal Lead.</note>

Take lead ore, or ceruse <term>cerusse: white lead, a pigment and chemical compound</term>, true white chalk and not adulterated <note>original: "fraudée," meaning mixed with cheaper fillers</note>, crush them well together, moistening them with distilled vinegar, then let them dry at their leisure; after it is dry, grind it once again, and place it in a glass vessel, pouring more distilled vinegar over it to the height of three or four fingers. Afterward, put your vessel in some warm place where no one travels <note>original: "personne ne trafique," suggesting a room without foot traffic or activity</note>, for the smoke <note>original: "fumée," referring here to the vapors or fumes</note> of this vinegar is bad and harmful. You may place it on warm ashes, letting the digestion <term>digestion: an alchemical process of gentle, continuous heating to promote chemical reaction</term> take place for the space of two full days, and stir it often. Note that while stirring it, or placing it on warm ashes, you must have your handkerchief before your nose, so as not to inhale this smoke. The vinegar will become tinted, and will take on a yellow color and a very sweet and pleasant flavor <note>Lead acetate is notoriously sweet—hence the name "Sugar of Saturn"—but it is highly toxic.</note>. I have warned you that the vessel must be of glass, for the strength of the vinegar would cause it to leak <note>original: "fuser," here meaning to seep through or dissolve the material</note> were it made of earthenware. After your vinegar has been tinted, draw it out, and replace it with more fresh vinegar, until it no longer colors and no longer becomes sweet. When this is done, remove your vinegar in a bath <note>original: "au bain," referring to a *balneum Mariae* or water bath used to evaporate the liquid</note>; the gum will remain at the bottom, upon which you must pour distilled rainwater; dissolve it once again, and the dregs <note>original: "feces," referring to the solid sediment or impurities</note> of the vinegar will remain at the bottom; continue to add more

### *Sperniolle, or Spermatic Composition*

Take frogspawn <note>original: "sperme de grenouilles"; historically, the jelly-like eggs of frogs were used in cooling remedies</note> in the month of March, and distill it in a water bath; it must be taken three days before the renewal of the Moon, for at that time, the resulting water does not smell bad.

### The virtues and use of the Sympathetic or celestial ointment.

This way of healing is not black magic as some fools and ignorant people believe, but rather [operates] through a certain attractive and magnetic virtue, caused by the Stars, which by the mediation of the air is drawn upon the wound, and is joined with it, so that the spiritual operation may show its effect.

It occurs, I say, because of the conjunction of the Stars and elements: for just as the heat of the Sun accords with the earth, so too the <term>persicaria</term> <note>Also known as smartweed or lady's thumb; Croll suggests a sympathetic link between the plant and the disease</note>, or <term>persicaire</term> with the disease, and when the Sun departs, the heat is also lost: it is therefore not wrong to believe that the same might happen in this case.

->*There are therefore three things which are*<-
->*caused by this ointment of such*<-
->*an admirable effect.*<-

First, the Sympathy of nature.
Secondly, the influence of the celestial bodies, which completes its operations through the mediation of the elements.
Thirdly, the natural balm that is within every man <note>The Paracelsian "internal balsam," a vital force believed to be responsible for the body's self-healing abilities</note>.

By this ointment, every kind of wound (in whatever manner they were made, or with whatever instrument they were caused, and in whichever sex it may be, provided that the nerves, or arteries, or any of the three principal members <note>In early modern medicine, these were typically the heart, brain, and liver</note>

In this matter, there is no need at all to sew the wound closed as <term>Surgeons</term> <note>At this time, surgeons were often distinct from university-trained physicians, focusing on manual operations and external treatments</note> usually do, but only to bandage it with a very clean linen cloth, moistened with the patient's own urine <note>In early modern medicine, urine was often used as a sterile wash for wounds</note>.

It is necessary that the person performing the cure abstain from women and from <term>pollution</term> <note>In this context, "pollution" refers to any sexual discharge or impurity, as the healer was expected to maintain a state of ritual or physical "purity" for the remedy to work</note> during the time they are working on it; however, before performing the anointing, it is very good to have stopped the bleeding of the wound.

For ruptures and fractures of the bones, one may add to this ointment a little powder of <term>Bugle</term> <note>Ajuga reptans, a plant traditionally used to stop bleeding</note>, or <term>consolide</term> <note>Also known as Comfrey (Symphytum officinale), famously used to "consolidate" or knit bones together</note>, or else powder of the roots of <term>black hellebore</term> <note>Helleborus niger, a potent medicinal plant used in varied preparations</note>.

->*A fine secret to know if the wounded person must strictly govern their eating and drinking.*<-

This is known when, upon the point of the instrument by which one was wounded, some drops or spots of blood appear; if none appear, he must take great care to govern himself well <note>This suggests that visible blood on the weapon acted as a diagnostic sign for the patient's internal state and dietary needs</note>.

Note, however, that if one cannot obtain the weapons by which the wound was made, one does not fail to perform the cure, but by another means.

One must have a small <term>sample of willow</term> <note>A splinter or small piece of willow wood</note>, soak and moisten it with the blood coming from the wound, and when the blood has dried of its own accord (without fire or sun), the said wood must be placed into the ointment that is in the <term>box</term> <note>original: "bouëtte," a small jar or apothecary's box</note>, and left there.

One can practice the same cure toward all other animals composed of flesh, blood, and bone.

->CONCLUSION.<-

Now let the brazen pride of the *Academic Thrasos* <note>original: "Thrasons," referring to Thraso, the boastful soldier from ancient comedy; used here to mock arrogant scholars who talk much but do little</note> come to an end: let them cease in the future (whenever they wish to extol themselves) from giving further rein to the violence of their threats, and stop mocking this divine science of our ancestors, the companion of truth, which they have until now despised. It is enough; let them no longer vilify the disciples of this great *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the Hermetic and alchemical tradition</note>, falsely accusing them of ignorance, envy, and fraud. Why do they demand ocular demonstrations and manifest preparations? No, no, it is not appropriate, it seems to me, for their "new science" to judge with such pride these secrets that I have brought to light—secrets given by divine goodness to the <term>Spagyric: <note>A term for alchemical medicine, from the Greek words meaning "to separate and to combine," referring to the process of purifying substances</note></term> republic, which they disdainfully call "charcoal-burning" <note>original: "charbonniere," a derogatory term used by university doctors to suggest alchemists were mere laborers or soot-covered furnace-tenders</note>. Meanwhile, I pray to the divine goodness that all those who, inspired by Heaven, shall use these secrets (having invoked the Supreme Power, that He might deign to bless their labor) may happily reach the end of their enterprise, returning the honor and glory to that **True Chemist** <note>Referring to God as the ultimate transformer and creator of nature</note> who judges our intentions and sees...

And so that this may be like a celestial decree, I offer my prayers to the Most Holy Trinity (which has given me the industry and will to bring to light these secrets or Spagyric seeds, not without great pain and labor) that it may ensure all posterity can feel the effects; it is not I alone who dedicates them to Him, but the entire Spagyric Senate <note>The "Spagyric Senate" refers to the collective community of alchemists and chemical physicians who follow the Hermetic tradition</note> with me. > *Has made its full effort; if by chance you can*
> *Surpass it, do so; otherwise, may this volume*
> *Always be favored by your kind regard.*

# VERY AMPLE TABLE OF THE
## *Royal Chemistry according to the Alphabetical order.*

->A<-

Complications of wounds are prevented by gums, namely, Galbanum, Opoponax, etc. 188. <note>original: "Accidens des playes." In early medicine, "accidents" refers to secondary symptoms or complications like infection or swelling. Galbanum and Opoponax are aromatic resins harvested from plants in the carrot family, used as antiseptic binders in plasters.</note>
Acidity of the oil of Vitriol prevents all putrefaction. 135 <note>original: "huille de Vitriol." This is highly concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>
Perfect balance of the elements is found in gold. 116 <note>original: "Adequation des elemens." Alchemists believed gold was the "perfect" metal because its constituent elements were perfectly balanced, making it resistant to decay or fire.</note>
Particular advice for extracting the oil of cinnamon. 72

# TREATISE
## ON SIGNATURES, OR
### The True Anatomy of the Great and Small World.

**A** I wish that the <term>botanists<note>original: "Botaniques"; referring here to the scholars of plant life during the Renaissance.</note></term> of our time, who, being ignorant of the internal form of herbs, recognize only their material substance, would devote their study as much to the knowledge of their <term>signatures<note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that the physical appearance of a plant—its shape, color, or texture—was a "signature" from God or nature indicating its medicinal purpose. For example, a plant with heart-shaped leaves might be used to treat heart ailments.</note></term> as they normally do to the naming of them. Upon these names, they base an infinity of vain disputes which can bring no profit to the <term>commonwealth of Medicine<note>A common early modern phrase referring to the collective community and shared knowledge of medical practitioners.</note></term>. 

But as many people (a thing that happens in all kinds of arts) have abandoned the marrow and kernel of science—in the manner of the common folk, who look only at the exterior—and do not wish to occupy themselves with anything but the bitterness of the bark; the result is that one finds an infinity of <term>herbalist-nomenclators<note>Scholars primarily focused on the cataloging and naming of plants rather than their occult or therapeutic properties.</note></term>. These people concern themselves with nothing else but describing the locations, names, and rinds of plants, claiming that this is where all their power lies, without noticing that the true and exact

This virtue, I say, is recognized more through the <term>signature<note>In this context, a "signature" is a physical mark or likeness on a plant that reveals its purpose—such as a leaf shaped like a liver being used to treat liver disease.</note></term>, or the analogical and mutual <term>sympathy<note>original: "sympathie analogique"; a Renaissance concept suggesting that things in nature are interconnected by hidden harmonies or "sympathies."</note></term> between the members of the human body and these plants, than by anything else. Furthermore, I am greatly astonished that they pass over in silence the proof which must be established through the <term>industry of fire<note>original: "l’industrie du feu"; this refers to alchemical practice, specifically the use of a furnace or heat to distill and analyze substances.</note></term> and the <term>anatomical knife<note>original: "couteau anatomique"; referring to the practice of dissecting plants to understand their internal structures, much like a surgeon dissects a body.</note></term>. # OF SIGNATURES.

<margin>One must not stop at the consideration of the quality of simples, but rather at their secret virtues.</margin>
...which must be examined, in order to have assurance of what is purgative, fragrant, and what might, for example, heal wounds or fevers. It is also in vain to dwell on the consideration of the <term>four qualities<note>The "four qualities"—heat, coldness, moisture, and dryness—formed the basis of traditional Galenic medicine, which the author here dismisses as "only the shadow of things."</note></term>, namely heat, coldness, humidity, and dryness; seeing as that is only the shadow of things, just like colors, which have neither roots nor power. This will never be denied by those who, as true physicians, recognize the virtues of <term>simples<note>A "simple" is a medicinal herb or plant used on its own to treat a specific ailment.</note></term> through the center of their root, and not by the surface of the bark; and who, setting aside the emptiness of the name, go to investigate the truth of things more exactly through profound speculation, and look among the secret traces of nature for the rarest virtues they have received from Heaven. Those, I say, recognize at first glance, by the mere sight of the surface of the herbs, with what faculties they are endowed; they know just as well what difference there is between the bark and the kernel as between the house and the <term>tenant<note>original: "inquilin"; from the Latin *inquilinus*, meaning a resident or lodger. The author uses this to describe the inner spirit or medicinal virtue dwelling within the physical plant.</note></term> (unless, of course, they wish to give the name of the statue to the stones and the wood, or leave the farmer to do the harvest with the hut). In all external things, the house is at least the dwelling of the internal virtues infused by the Almighty, just as the body is that of the soul. It seems to me that that Philosopher walked very surely, who, to judge the spirit and understanding of a man, did not amuse himself with the name, but with the word, as the true character...

# PREFACE

...of man; and indeed, seeing one day a young youth stand before him without saying a word, he said to him, "Speak, oh child, so that I may know you." Thus, the secret movements of the understanding are manifested by the voice; in the same way, does it not seem that herbs speak to the inquisitive physician through their <term>signature<note>The "doctrine of signatures" was a historical belief that plants resembling parts of the human body could be used to treat ailments of those parts.</note></term>, revealing to him through some resemblance their internal virtues, hidden beneath the veil of nature's silence? Also (if I use the words of the learned <note>original: "B. Aporta"; Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar and polymath whose work *Phytognomonica* explored how the appearance of plants revealed their healing properties.</note>), this is a means which the Supreme Goodness often employs to manifest the divine secrets hidden in the deepest <term>depths<note>original: "entrailles"; literally "entrails" or "bowels," here referring to the innermost essence of natural things.</note></term> of natural things; which nevertheless seem to have some signature of divine ideas. Thus, He could not (in my judgment) find a more suitable and admirable way than that; for let us suppose that plants could speak for themselves, and tell of the admirable and secret virtues with which nature has enriched them; surely they would not be understood by everyone, nor their powers so well manifested as they are by the "writings" known to all the world. Otherwise, it would have been necessary for the plants to all exist within a single nation, or else for them to have spoken in every kind of language. It is therefore enough that wise nature subtly manifests her power through some sympathy and signature known to everyone. Is it not true that all herbs, plants, trees, and others coming from the depths of the earth, are so many books and signs...

# ON SIGNATURES.

...magical <note>Continuing the thought from the previous page: "It would have been necessary for the plants to be [magical] writings..."</note>, communicated by the infinite mercy of God? <margin>The virtues of plants are diversified according to the diversity of climates and regions.</margin>
Each region contains within itself the matrix of its element <note>In alchemical thought, the "matrix" is the specialized environment or "womb" within an element (like earth or water) where specific life or minerals are generated.</note> and provides for itself what is necessary; this is why nature has sought to provide and temper the **simples** appropriate to each sky, climate, country, region, and age; not forgetting in these the difference of sex, just as among sentient beings. And as divine providence has distinguished (and not without cause) anatomy into male and female, so too must one be careful in application not to confuse the sex, so that they may operate with more vigor: for just as man and woman are of a different nature, so too are remedies. I do not speak of "hermaphroditic" medicines, but rather of **simples** in their nature, some of which are suited for young people, others for the decrepit and those bowed under the weight of old age, which is clearly seen in the **Hellebores** <note>A group of flowering plants used since antiquity to treat "madness" and various ailments, though they are highly toxic if not handled with expert care.</note>. ### OF SIGNATURES. ###

<margin>

God is the Being of the stars, that is to say the place, the origin, and the <term>complication<note>In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the way all things are "enfolded" or contained within God before they are "unfolded" into the world.</note></term> of all creatures, from whom everything has come, and to whom everything naturally wants to return.

Now, therefore, all visible bodies with the elements are in the Stars, and the Stars in the visible bodies; the Stars are in the Angels, and the Angels in the Stars; the Angels are in God, and God in the Angels; but in such a way that the superior can exist without the inferior, but not the inferior without the superior. Neither bodies nor the visible world could subsist without the Stars, nor the Stars without the essence of the Angels; and the Angels also would not be if the uncreated God were not, from whom they draw their dependence. 

By knowing God, one knows the Angels, inasmuch as they are the perfect Image of God; by knowing the Angels, one has no doubt of the Stars, the knowledge of which gives us a certain science of all created bodies—that is to say, of the visible world, in which is comprised the <term>Microcosm<note>The "little world"; a common term for a human being, seen as a miniature map of the entire universe.</note></term>, as its natural and legitimate son; inasmuch as "as is the father, so is the son." By this same means, though proceeding backward, we are led from visible things to invisible things, because all things move from the interior to the exterior: for Angelic substances depend on God; the Stars—that is, the invisible virtue of things—depend on the Angels; and from the Stars come the visible forms that make up bodies.

Angels are most certain mirrors, without being subject to corruption, having been stripped of it by divine goodness.
</margin>

And just as all things are in God divinely, so they are in the Angels Angelically, and corporally or worldly in the world: for as light is among the darkness, so also the superior is among the inferior; and vice-versa.

## TO THE READER.

Dear Reader, I wished to conduct a search for the names of the plants in these signatures, which might satisfy your curiosity in some way. I have provided them in English <note>original: "François" — the author lists French, Latin, Greek, Italian, Spanish, German, Flemish, and Arabic.</note>, Latin, Greek, Italian, Spanish, German, Flemish, and Arabic; however, there are some which do not have all these names, of which I wanted to notify you beforehand. ### Of the kidneys.

<margin>The names.</margin>

<header>ON DISEASES.</header>

...on account of its signature.

### *Of Colic.*

The **bindweed** <term>convolvulus: a climbing plant known for its twisting, winding stems</term> which grows among the wheat represents the intestines; for this reason, having prepared it as a decoction, it is a remarkable remedy for colic.
The eel is a true plague <note>likely meaning it is either a cause of the ailment or a "bane" that destroys the disease</note> for colic.

### *Of Scars.*

The olive tree.
The elms.
And every kind of tree bearing clusters <note>original: *raisins*, referring generally to fruit clusters like grapes or berries</note> which have split bark are very certain remedies both for wounds and for scars.

### *Of Dysentery.*

The root of the **yellow water-iris** <term>acorus aquatique: likely the yellow flag iris, *Iris pseudacorus*</term>, gathered in the month of May and placed upon the region of the stomach <term>ventricule: the stomach or belly</term>, is an excellent remedy for dysentery; for it bears the signature and color of the excrement.
The seeds of the **elder** <note>original: *sambuc* or *suyer* (sureau)</note> perform the same function.

### *Of Erysipelas.* <note>A painful, red bacterial skin infection, historically known as "St. Anthony’s Fire"</note>

A decoction made from the seed of the **sharp-pointed dock** <term>oxylapathon: a species of wild sorrel or dock plant</term>, which has the color of flesh—not entirely red—is a very certain remedy for erysipelas.
The **colcothar of vitriol** <term>red iron oxide residue produced by heating metallic sulfates</term>, calcined <note>heated to a high temperature</note> with intensity and dissolved with plantain water, when applied externally, also works wonders for it.
The **marsh iris** <note>original: *acorus de marest*</note> has the same virtues for erysipelas.

<header>ON THE SIGNATURE</header>

### *On Epilepsy.*

**Oak mistletoe** <note>original: *guy de chesne*. Mistletoe growing on oak trees was considered particularly sacred and potent in ancient and early modern medicine</note> causes the disease to die.

### *On Scales of the Feet.*

Iron scales <note>Flakes of iron oxide produced when hammering hot iron</note> bear the signature of those [scales] which appear on the feet or the lips; for just as this crust is pushed to the surface by heat, so too by the art of nature the separation of waste from minerals occurs in the human body; for which reason <term>crocus Martis</term> <note>original: "crocus Martis," a red iron oxide powder used in early medicine</note> and <term>oil of Mars</term> <note>original: "l'huille de Mars," a preparation of iron chloride</note> are very beneficial in such instances.

### *On Spasms.*

White snails possess a certain stone <note>Likely the "snail-stone" or small internal shell found in some mollusks, historically used as a charm or ground into medicine</note> which, when administered, greatly serves those who are subject to such an ailment.
The hock <note>the joint in the hind leg</note> of a hare has the same effects as the snail-stone for the aforementioned illness.

### *On Abscesses Forming in the Throat.*

The root of the <term>gladiolus</term> <note>the sword lily</note> has certain swellings which are of great use in curing the said disease.
The root of the herb called <term>scrofularia</term> <note>Figwort</note> is furthermore very well-suited for it because of its signature: for it is entirely covered in small bumps which naturally represent these <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apostumes," or inflammatory swellings</note>. Thus, it is used with great satisfaction for the healing of <term>scrofulous ulcers</term> <note>original: "ulceres strumeux," referring to swellings of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis of the neck</note> arising from a cold humor <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids that governed health; a "cold" humor was thought to cause sluggish, swollen conditions</note>; for it softens them to the great relief of the patient, as well as the satisfaction of the physician.
The fig tree is also very useful for this, because of the resemblance it bears to these scrofulous swellings.

### *signature.*

Previously we have dealt with the <term>signature</term> <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that the physical appearance of a plant or mineral—its color, shape, or texture—revealed its medicinal use.</note> of plants and diseases, which by a certain sympathy heal the diseases and infirmities for which they are appropriate, and of which they bear the signature. <header>OF SIGNATURES.</header>

## From where men have derived their
## signatures.

<margin>Love loves its like.</margin>
Firstly, bold and courageous men derive their signature <term>Signature: From the "Doctrine of Signatures," a Renaissance belief that every object in the natural world carries a physical sign or "signature" from God that indicates its purpose, medicinal use, or inner character.</term> from the Lion and the Eagle.

Faithful friends [derive theirs] from dolphins, whose fidelity toward men is well enough known and described among histories both ancient and modern. <note>The author likely refers to classical myths, such as the story of the poet Arion who was saved by a dolphin, or Pliny the Elder’s accounts of dolphins befriending humans.</note>

The sign of a constant friendship is recognized in the pig, which, grunting from some wound or otherwise, excites all the others to do the same; a thing which does not happen among dogs, seeing that immediately the others band together against the one who has been wounded, as being the weakest.

True and constant friends are further represented by ivy, which (after its death) does not cease to clasp and embrace the tree with which it was nourished and raised.

Fraudulent and hypocritical friends are very well signified to us by crocodiles, which, under the pretense of weeping, deceive those who, out of pity, make their way to their rescue. <note>This is a reference to the "crocodile tears" myth, popularized in the Middle Ages by bestiaries claiming that crocodiles wept to lure prey or felt mock-sorrow while devouring it.</note>

Inconstant and fickle Court friends, who are only friends during the favor of fortune, are represented by migratory birds, which leave us as soon as winter begins to be felt.

# ON SIGNATURES. 99

The ignorant and arrogant [are represented] by those same ears of grain, but empty of seed: for they raise their heads above the others, as if they were something great; furthermore, they are also represented by the scum of the pot, which always wants to float above the meat, without realizing that it is worth nothing. The empty vessel represents them well: for as long as it is being handled, it makes a louder sound than one that is full.

The simple, without malice, by the **dove**.

The crafty and cunning by the **stingray**, which seeks only to destroy those who swim around it. <note>original: *pastenade marine*. Likely the stingray or "sea pastinaca," which early naturalists described as using its tail to strike and poison fishermen and other sea creatures.</note>

The "sleepers" [sluggards] by the **hedgehog**, and the **dormouse**, animals which during the winter sleep in such a way that fire can hardly wake them; even if dismembered, they cannot be awakened, unless they are placed in a boiling pot: for instantly the severed limbs show by their movement that the animal was not yet dead.

<margin>One must give credit to the historians.</margin>
As for me, I believe that these animals have given their **signature** to the Russians <note>original: *Rusciens*. The author refers to a common 16th-century travel myth, popularized by writers like Sigismund von Herberstein, claiming that people in certain parts of Muscovy (Russia) underwent a form of hibernation, "dying" in winter and "thawing" back to life in spring.</note> (to say nothing of the storks and swallows submerged in winter, which, according to the reports of fishermen, return to life in the spring) <note>At this time, it was a widely held scientific belief that swallows did not migrate but instead hibernated in mud at the bottom of ponds.</note> who, during the severity of the winter, seem to be dead among the forests, and then come back to life with the arrival of spring. Animals which remain all winter in their caves without eating, living off their own substance, represent these "sleepers" quite aptly.

### *How we acquired the use of emetics*
### *& purgatives.*

As for the use of **emetics** <note>original: *vomitifs*; substances used to induce vomiting</note>, it was given to us by dogs, which, when they are sick, eat **couch-grass** <note>original: *grame*; likely *Agropyron repens*, commonly known as dog-grass, which animals use to induce purging</note>; this has the power to purge them not only by vomiting but also through the bowels.

The **gull** <note>original: *laro*; from the Latin *larus*, referring to a sea-gull or sea-mew</note>, an aquatic bird, has another method for purging itself: for feeling its stomach too heavily burdened, it seeks out a tree where it can find two branches very close to each other, and then places itself between the two and forces itself through, which compels it to surrender what it has in its stomach.

The **crow** <note>original: *corbeau*; can refer to a crow or a raven</note>, an insatiable bird, when it has taken its meal upon some carcass and feels that its digestive faculties do not have enough heat to achieve **concoction** <note>original: *concoction*; in pre-modern medicine, this was the process of "cooking" or digesting food within the body to turn it into useful humors</note>, also goes to squeeze itself between two tree branches, as mentioned above, or else between two stones or a split rock. By this means, it forces out the excrement, as much through the internal part as the posterior, leaving in its body only the **nutritive humor** <note>original: *humeur alimentaire*; the refined substance extracted from food during digestion</note>, or pure substance; this is the reason it lives longer than any animal in the world.

112 THE CORRESPONDENCE

<margin>
The **halcyons** and other birds of **Egypt** called **ibis** have great secrets for maintaining their youth, which they do not go to fetch or seek anywhere else but from within themselves, according to **Romans 8:21–22**. <note>original: "Romains 8. fect. 21. 22." This biblical passage speaks of creation being liberated from its "bondage to decay."</note>
</margin>
...the **silk-worm**, they hold the first rank. I pass over in silence the **halcyon** <note>original: *alcyõ*; a mythical bird often identified with the kingfisher, believed to have the power to calm the sea and renew itself</note> which feeds on the primary essences, renewing its skin and feathers every year after its death; flies and bats testify to this as well, which, having remained all winter as if buried, seem to be resurrected in the Spring by the favor of the temperate air.

<margin>
This **regeneration** of animals is more of a **transplantation**, the root always remaining, which is made and grafted upon the trunk.
</margin>
The **ant**, wise and prudent among all other animals, possesses this gift of nature: the knowledge that after its current age, it must arrive at a better state. This is why it strives with all its courage, so that after so much toil it may find rest. This is easily granted to it by Mother Nature as a reward for its past labors; in its old age, she presents it with two wings, and by this means metamorphoses a crawling animal into a flying insect <note>original: *mouche volante*; literally "flying fly," here referring to winged ants</note>, allowing it to rest and grant a truce to its hardships.

We see the same thing occur with **silk-worms**, which, hatched from a small seed <note>original: *femence*; referring to the eggs of the silkworm</note>, emerge as little worms. But having finished their natural course and "rotted" within the skin of the worm, nature causes them to be resurrected as a small white butterfly, rewarding them in this way for their past work. As for me, I have studied with brevity to manifest the most hidden secrets of nature to those who are curious to know them, whom I heartily pray to hold them in high regard, and following my example...

### ->OF SIGNATURES.<-

...delve further into it; for having reached the goal of their intention, they will receive an unparalleled satisfaction, marvelling at the bounties of nature. It is quite true that in this place, I have done nothing but clear the path; nevertheless, it has been with as much faithfulness as the affection I have for serving everyone. As for **signatures** <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was a theory that plants resembling parts of the body or specific symbols could treat related ailments or revealed divine mysteries.</note>, I am content to say in passing that that of our first father **Adam** is found in **wheat**, just as the mysteries of the **Virgin** are found in the artificial cut of the **vine**, and the **two-headed eagle** and other mysteries in the root of the **fern** when cut in different ways. Likewise, **lightning** is found in the roots of both types of **victorialis** <note>original: *victorialle*; likely *Allium victorialis*, a mountain leek believed to protect against injury and lightning</note> gathered at a certain time. I do not wish to forget the herb called <term>crosswort</term> <note>original: *cruciata*; likely *Gentiana cruciata*, named for its cross-shaped leaves and believed to protect against weapons</note>, which resists the force of arms; these being, nonetheless, all magic and natural signs known only to the lovers of this art. I do not wish to go any further, lest I give cause for mockery to the **sophists** and to those with dark souls prone to ill-thinking; for were that to happen, I would be frustrated in my design, seeing as I neither hope nor desire anything but to satisfy those fine spirits. If, however, I see that this little treatise is viewed favorably, I will endeavor to bring others to light which might provide much more satisfaction and profit; for I hope to demonstrate briefly that which concerns <term>magnetic healing</term> <note>A theory of healing involving the "sympathy" or attraction between substances, popularized by Paracelsus</note>, natural Magic, and the study of characters.

Secondly, at what time and constellation...

the time when medicines should be made and gathered.

Thirdly, the manner of curing enchantments and spells <note>original: *malefices*; harmful magic intended to cause injury or misfortune</note>, and the knowledge of them.

Fourthly, the proof of several diseases with certain knowledge and prediction of death, or the future health of the sick.

Friend reader, this was the intention of our **Crollius** <note>Oswald Croll (c. 1563–1609) was a German physician and alchemist who popularized the "Doctrine of Signatures," the idea that plants reveal their medicinal uses through their physical appearance.</note> if God had not wished to house him in His Paradise, unwilling to permit men to become prideful of this beautiful science, which would have made them forget the worship and honor they owe Him.

It is therefore to You, All-Powerful, to whom we owe the obligation for all that we have been able to do in this mortal voyage, seeing that it has only been by Your favor; for it is impossible for us even to breathe without You. It is You who leads us to the port and true haven of salvation.
